paras: The peonage case of Charlie Warren was a federal prosecution begun in August 1905, when J. K. Mitchell, a farmer of Wilcox County, Georgia, was arrested on a charge of holding Warren, a fifteen-year-old Black boy, in servitude. Mitchell was jailed at Macon to await a hearing, and the arrest was carried as a brief wire item by papers from Maine to Virginia.

According to a fuller Macon dispatch, Mitchell had brought the boy to his farm from North Georgia. The boy later "became indebted to his employer and ran away," and he was pursued with a warrant taken out in a justice court. Rather than let the case proceed, Mitchell was "said to have paid the costs incurred and afterwards made the boy labor on his farm."

A warrant was issued from the district attorney's office charging Mitchell with "working Charlie Warren, a negro boy aged 15, in servitude." Federal officers arrested Mitchell at his home on Monday, August 14, 1905, and that night lodged him in the Bibb County jail at Macon. His hearing on the peonage charge was set for the following day in Macon.
No report of the hearing, an indictment, a trial or any outcome appears in the coverage, nor any account from Warren himself.

The story reached readers almost entirely as short dispatches datelined Macon, printed in papers outside Georgia. On August 15 the Richmond Times Dispatch ran it under "Charged With Peonage," calling Mitchell "a prominent farmer of Willecox county," while the Daily Kennebec Journal of Maine folded it into a column of condensed dispatches. The New York Evening World, in a news-in-brief column headed "Peonage in Georgia," described Mitchell as "a rich farmer" and put the charge bluntly as holding the boy "as a slave."

A longer version headed "Arrested For Peonage," which added the account of the boy's debt and the justice-court warrant, appeared in the Virginia Gazette on August 19 and the Edgefield Advertiser of South Carolina on August 23, both spelling the boy's name "Warrne." These reports named the boy's race but not Mitchell's, and none carried editorial comment. No coverage of the case in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Peonage case of Charlie Warren
bases: Federal officers arrested Mitchell on a charge of peonage for working a Black boy 'in servitude' after paying the costs of a warrant against him for debt (A2, A4).

Every report (A1-A5) traces to Macon dispatches about the federal arrest, with no local Georgia, court or Black-press account to corroborate it independently; the reports do agree on the arrest and charge.

accounts.gist: Mitchell was said to have brought the boy from North Georgia; when the indebted boy ran away and was pursued with a justice-court warrant, Mitchell paid the costs instead of letting the law take its course and then made him work on his farm.

framing.detail: Brief neutral dispatches under headlines such as 'Charged With Peonage' and 'Arrested For Peonage', identifying the victim only as 'a negro boy' and the accused as a 'prominent farmer'.
The New York Evening World headed its item 'Peonage in Georgia' and put the charge plainly as holding the boy 'as a slave'.
